children: It’s the ultimate sellers’ market for crude oil. Yet Saudi Arabia’s oil giant Aramco has just slashed the flagship crude price for Asian buyers to $5 a barrel below the Dubai/Oman benchmark. This isn’t wild generosity on the part of the Saudis. It’s effectively a rebate to compensate buyers for the extraordinary costs and risks of getting the oil out of the Gulf.

The Wall Street Journal reckons VLCCs, the giant tankers that carry two million barrels of crude, are charging as much as $40 million for a round trip in and out of the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz. Even crews are cashing in, with Indian and other sailors getting bonuses of up to $25,000, equivalent to a full year’s normal salary, for the journey.

But here’s the surprise. Despite all the danger and disruption, Gulf oil is flowing again, with shipments at 80 per cent of pre-war levels thanks to US naval protection and strikes that knocked out Iranian radar and communications along the waterway.

Around three million barrels a day (bpd) from Middle Eastern producers reached India in September, with Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Kuwait once again supplying large quantities. That’s pushed total crude imports to 5.3 million bpd, the highest this year and broadly back to pre-war levels. The Gulf producers, India’s main suppliers before cheap Russian oil flooded the market following the Ukraine invasion, are suddenly back in business.

So where does that leave Russia, whose oil helped keep India humming through the worst months of the Hormuz crisis? In June and July, Russia supplied roughly half of India’s crude, with purchases peaking at 2.65 million bpd in July. By September, Russian imports dropped to 1.75 million bpd, their lowest since April.

Part of the explanation is there was simply more Middle Eastern oil available. “Middle East barrels regained share as availability and logistics improved,” says Sumit Ritolia, senior analyst at trade consultancy Kpler.

But something else happened. China came roaring back into the market for Russian oil. During the early stages of the Hormuz crisis, China sharply reduced its crude purchases just as the rest of Asia was scrambling for supplies. Beijing entered the crisis with enormous oil stockpiles and appears to have relied heavily on those reserves while its refineries cut back production.

China is now buying aggressively again, putting it into direct competition with India for Russian barrels. Traditionally, the two countries have bought somewhat different Russian grades. China takes large quantities of ESPO crude shipped from Russia’s Pacific ports, while India has become the dominant buyer of Urals crude shipped from western Russia.

But China has also been looking for Urals. That means Indian refiners suddenly have a formidable rival for the very barrels they have come to depend on. When India first started massively buying Russian oil in 2022, Moscow desperately needed new customers for crude that could no longer easily be sold in Europe because of Western sanctions. Russian crude came with such hefty discounts that it remained a bargain even after paying to ship it thousands of extra kilometres to Indian refineries.

That bargain has largely disappeared. Russian oil that once came at a steep discount has at times been selling at a premium in today’s exceptionally tight market. Yet India cannot simply walk away from Russia. It imports close to 90 per cent of the crude it consumes and needs enormous quantities every day. There simply aren’t many producers capable of replacing Russian volumes at short notice.

And that brings us to the multibillion-dollar question hanging over India’s oil trade: what does Washington do next? The US has threatened up to 100 per cent sanctions on countries buying Russian energy, putting India and China, the two biggest Russian crude purchasers, in the firing line. Beijing has plenty of ways to retaliate. India is a much easier target, particularly when New Delhi and Washington are at a trade stalemate.
That raises the possibility India could once again come under intense US pressure to cut its Russian purchases further. Fortunately for India, more Gulf oil is getting through.

For Indian refiners, the turmoil has created winners and losers. Reliance Industries is one of the biggest winners. Its giant Jamnagar complex buys crude, turns it into petrol, diesel and other fuels and sells those products. With refining margins soaring, it’s become an extremely lucrative business.

India’s state-owned refiners face a much tougher situation. Indian Oil, BPCL and HPCL are having to buy increasingly expensive crude and fuel on world markets. But petrol and diesel prices at Indian pumps haven’t risen to match those higher costs. That means they’re being forced to absorb the difference.

A few months ago, the overriding worry was whether India could find enough crude. Now India is having to juggle its old suppliers in the Gulf, its crucial new supplier in Russia, a resurgent China competing for the same barrels and the worry of US sanctions.

title: The great oil switch
